To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the sample complexity of kernel regression can be improved by a factor equal the size of the symmetry group, when the kernel is invariant to that group, and that this can be extended to the setting of stability to small deformation, modeled as a set of permutations.

the sample complexity of a learning problem is improved by a factor equaling the size of an invariance group, and that this result extends to geometric stability to small perturbations, modeled as subsets of permutations.

In summary, our research is concerned with
the sample complexity of kernel methods for learning under invariance and geometric stability.
the sample complexity of kernel-based learning algorithms when the target function presents certain symmetries and/or is geometrically stable.
the sample complexity of supervised learning problems, where the target function is assumed to have certain geometric stability properties, such as invariants or small perturbations.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the sample complexity of the learning problem is improved by a factor of the size of the invariance group, and that this result is also valid for geometric stability.

the sample complexity of kernel learning problems is reduced by a factor proportional to the size of a group when the target function is invariant under the group, and is reduced by a similar factor proportional to the cardinality of a subset of permutations when the target function presents geometric stability under the subset.

the sample complexity of kernel learning improves when the data are generated by a process with geometric priors such as translation or permutation invariance, or geometric stability to small perturbations, provided that these priors are reflected in the choice of the kernel.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we provide a framework for studying the sample complexity of kernel-based learning algorithms when the data is high-dimensional, the target function has some invariance or stability properties, and the sample size is small.
we study the sample complexity for kernel-based learning methods when the target function is assumed to have some geometric stability, which is a natural property for a variety of problems.
we provide a general theory for the sample complexity of geometric stability and invariance in learning problems, and we show how it can be used to improve the efficiency of kernel methods.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, when the target function presents certain geometric properties, it is often possible to learn it with a significantly smaller sample complexity, by exploiting the geometry of the problem.
, when the sample complexity is high enough, geometric priors can be used to reduce the number of samples needed to learn.

geometric priors, such as in the form of invariance or stability, are not only useful to make efficient use and reduce dimensionality of the input data, but also have a significant impact on the sample complexity of the learning problem at hand.
